title: What does a healthy night's sleep actually look like? | Terra
summary: What 159,000 people's sleep reveals about the night linked to the lowest resting heart rate: about eight hours, a 10pm bedtime, and a regular schedule.
body_markdown:
## Duration and bedtime: mostly pointing the same way


***Figure 1:** The night that sits next to a lower heart rate, and next to more steps. Top row, resting heart rate. Bottom row, daily steps. The open circle is the “best” bin in that panel. Larger points are more people. August–October 2026.*


Resting heart rate is lowest at eight to eight and a half hours, at 58.0 bpm, and at a bedtime of about 10 pm, around 58 bpm. Only slightly higher at 8 pm, and nearly 64 by 3 am.


Raw daily steps peak a bit earlier, at seven to seven and a half hours, about 7,850 steps. That is mostly because those people are awake for about an hour longer. To state the obvious, you can only take steps while you are awake, so I split each person's steps by the hours they are up: 24 minus time asleep. Steps per waking hour peak at the same eight to eight and a half hours, about 480 an hour.


Earlier bedtimes win on steps as well: about 8,500 at 8 pm, falling to about 6,100 at 3 am. Going to bed at 8 pm in this sample does not shorten the day, because those people tend to wake earlier too. The[last post](https://tryterra.co/research/what-time-do-morning-exercisers-go-to-bed) showed wake-up time shifting much less than bedtime, so a later bedtime usually means less sleep, not more.


Past nine hours, both the heart rate and the steps look worse. That is the classic J-curve. The right-hand rise is not evidence that too much sleep has negative consequences. It is quite probable that people who are slightly unwell, or less healthy, spend longer asleep, with the same poor health lifting the resting heart rate and cutting the steps.


It's the same problem that has plagued many large-scale health studies, especially alcohol. It can look as if drinking some is better for mortality than none. In fact, the statistics may reflect people who stopped because they were already ill and were then counted in the "none" group (Stockwell et al., 2016).


The National Sleep Foundation puts healthy adults at 7 to 9 hours (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015). The mortality research tends to look the same (Cappuccio et al., 2010). Short sleep and long sleep both track with higher risk, and the long arm is usually read as illness, not as a reason to sleep less.


## Not one habit, three


The worry is that I have counted the same person three times. Go to bed later and you also tend to sleep a bit less, and the bedtime moves around a bit more. If that was the whole story, any one of the three charts would do. The heat maps hold one still, so you can see whether the others are still there.


***Figure 2:** Bedtime against total sleep, and bedtime against regularity. Rows are the usual bedtime, 8 pm at the top. Across the top of the left pair, hours asleep. Across the top of the right pair, how much the bedtime moves. A blank cell has fewer than 100 people. Darker red is a higher resting heart rate. Darker blue is more steps.*


Start on the left, with heart rate. The lower heart rates sit around 7.5 to 8.5 hours on almost every row, and the whole row gets worse once bedtime is past midnight. Eight hours at 10 pm and eight hours at 2 am are not the same. You can't cancel out a 2 am bedtime by sleeping eight hours, and an early bedtime does not make up for a very short night.


The steps map below it tells the same story: the most walking sits around 7 to 8 hours, in the earlier bedtimes, and fades when the night gets very long or bedtime gets later.


The right-hand pair has no best stripe down the middle. Heart rate gets worse as the bedtime wanders, and worse as it gets later. The busiest corner for steps is early and tight. An early bedtime that swings by three hours isn't the same as a steady one.


***Figure 3:** The same bedtime-by-sleep grid, split by how much the bedtime moves. Left, under one hour. Middle, one to two hours. Right, over two hours.*


The valley in heart rate, and the hill in steps, are still there when you split the grid by regularity. Regularity does not create them. What it does is move the level of the whole grid. When the bedtime stays within an hour, heart rate sits lower and steps sit higher, at the same length of night. When it moves by more than two hours, the grid is warmer and the walking is thinner.


## Regularity: the cleanest variable, and where good enough sits


Regularity is a straight line. More regular is better. I write that consistency is key in most of my blogs, but even I am surprised by how straight it actually is.


Sleep length and bedtime can both be too little and too much. Regularity is different. It is how many minutes the bedtime moves, and the smallest that number can be is zero, the same time every night. You cannot have a negative spread, so there is no point on the other side of zero where being even more regular starts to look worse.


Across the people in this sample, from about half an hour of spread out to about three hours, a wider spread just stays worse.


Moving from a spread of over three hours to under 45 minutes takes heart rate from 62.7 to 57.6 bpm, and steps from about 6,900 to about 8,300.


Bedtime spread People Resting heart rate Steps


Under 15 min 231 56.7 9,506


15–20 min 601 57.4 8,517


20–25 min 1,438 57.1 8,517


25–30 min 3,166 57.1 8,534


30–35 min 5,329 57.3 8,366


35–40 min 7,722 57.7 8,213


40–45 min 10,164 58.1 8,094


45–60 min 36,918 58.7 7,915


***Table 1. The tight end of bedtime regularity. Each row is how much that person's own bedtimes move.***


From 45 minutes down to about 25, tighter still lines up with a lower heart rate and more steps. Between 15 and 30 minutes the two numbers level off, near 57 bpm and about 8,500 steps. The 231 people under 15 minutes look a bit better again. That group is too small to hang the conclusion on.


The gains flatten out once you're within about 30 minutes. That plateau might be a bit like the J-curve, or it might just be a small-sample effect at the very tight end. I also think it is a practical one. Most people in real life have some variation in their bedtime, and you don't need Bryan Johnson-level rigidity to get almost all of the upside.


## What I'd take from it


None of this is a person changing tonight and watching these benefits appear tomorrow. The[last post](https://tryterra.co/research/what-time-do-morning-exercisers-go-to-bed) found that, for the same person, one late night barely moves the next morning. These are people who already live this way.


In my triathlon training, the answer was not to focus too much on one discipline. It was to keep all three in balance, and adjust whichever one had slipped. I would do the same here.


The wrong thing to do is to pick one night, or one number, and call it the protocol. Keep sleep around seven and a half to eight and a half hours, keep bedtime close to 10 pm, and as regular as possible.


## FAQs


### How much sleep is linked to the lowest resting heart rate?


Resting heart rate is lowest at eight to eight and a half hours, at 58.0 bpm.


### Do people who sleep more walk more?


Not as a daily total. Daily steps peak at seven to seven and a half hours of sleep, about 7,850, mostly because those people are awake longer. Steps per waking hour peak at the same eight to eight and a half hours as the lowest heart rate, about 480 per hour. Past nine hours, the step count falls to about 6,000.


### What is the best bedtime?


Heart rate is lowest at a 10 pm bedtime, at about 58 bpm, only slightly higher at 8 pm, and nearly 64 by 3 am. Steps are highest at 8 pm, at about 8,500, and fall to about 6,100 at 3 am.


### How regular does bedtime need to be?


More regular looks better down to a spread of about half an hour. Moving from over three hours of spread to under 45 minutes takes heart rate from 62.7 to 57.6 bpm and steps from about 6,900 to about 8,300. Tighter than about 30 minutes, once the groups are large, there is no clear further gain.


### How much sleep do I need?


There isn't one perfect night. The National Sleep Foundation puts healthy adults at 7 to 9 hours. In this data, heart rate and steps per waking hour look best at eight to eight and a half hours, with an earlier rather than later bedtime, and a regular window of about half an hour.
